pos: n. (Julian the Apostate, Roman emperor 361–363, raised a Christian, who renounced the faith and attempted to restore paganism)
etymology: Latin Julianus. Nephew of Constantine, baptised and educated in the church, he declared for the old gods on becoming sole emperor and died on campaign in Persia two years later.
biblical_def: Julian is the church's standing example of an emperor's apostasy, and Scripture supplies the categories rather than the name. Hebrews states the hardest case: “it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift… if they shall fall away, to renew them again unto repentance” (Heb 6:4–6). John supplies the interpretation: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us” (1Jn 2:19). The parable gives the mechanism: the stony ground hearer receives the word with joy, “yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while” (Mat 13:20–21). And a named case stands in the canon: “Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world” (2Ti 4:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines apostasy as an abandonment of what one has professed; a total desertion, or departure from one's faith or religion.
webster_full: APOSTASY, n. An abandonment of what one has professed; a total desertion, or departure from one's faith or religion.
APOSTATE, n. One who has forsaken the church, sect or profession to which he before adhered.
In its original sense, applied to one who has abandoned his religion; but correlatively, one who has abandoned his party or principles.
scriptures: Heb 6:4
For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost,

They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us: but they went out, that they might be made manifest that they were not all of us.
But he that received the seed into stony places, the same is he that heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it;
For Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world, and is departed unto Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia, Titus unto Dalmatia.
Yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended.
corruption_summary: Apostasy is imagined as a sudden defection, and the New Testament describes a root that was never there.
corruption_paragraphs: Julian's case is instructive precisely because it was not sudden. He was baptised, catechised, and served as a reader in the church; his defection was worked out over years of private study before it was declared, and when it came it was not a collapse into vice but a deliberate programme of restoration, conducted by a disciplined and personally austere man. That is the shape apostasy usually has. It is rarely a moral scandal and often an intellectual and social migration, completed inwardly long before anyone notices.

First John 2:19 gives the church's settled reading of such cases and it is neither triumphalist nor despairing: they went out from us, but they were not of us. John's argument is that the departure revealed rather than caused the state — they went out that they might be made manifest that they were not all of us. This is how the Reformed have held perseverance without denying the reality of what a congregation watches happen: the elect are kept, and a visible profession is not the same thing as election, and only the end of a life shows which was present.

Hebrews 6 remains the hardest passage in the New Testament and honesty requires saying so. The Reformed reading is that its subject is a professor who has come very near — enlightened, tasted, partaker, tasted the good word — without ever being made a partaker of Christ, and that the writer's own next sentence supports it: but, beloved, we are persuaded better things of you, and things that accompany salvation. The warning is real and is one of the means by which believers are kept. A man frightened by it is not its subject; the man it describes reads it without disturbance.
roots_summary: Greek apostasia (G646), a falling away; parapipto (G3895), to fall away; egkataleipo (G1459), to forsake, abandon; rhiza (G4491), root.
roots_lines: Greek apostasia (G646) — falling away, apostasy; 2 Thessalonians 2:3, Acts 21:21.
Greek parapipto (G3895) — to fall away; Hebrews 6:6 only.
Greek egkatelipen (G1459) — hath forsaken; 2 Timothy 4:10, 4:16, Hebrews 13:5 — where God says He never will.
usage: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” — the departure revealed it.
“Hath not root in himself” — and it received the word with joy.
“Having loved this present world” — a named case, in the canon.

pos: n. pl. (those who deny or live without God; the AV renders the Greek atheoi as “without God in the world”)
etymology: Greek a-, without, and theos, God. The one New Testament occurrence is Ephesians 2:12, and it is said of Gentiles who had many gods — which tells us what the Bible means by the word.
biblical_def: The Greek atheoi appears once and describes the Ephesians before conversion: they were “without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world” (Eph 2:12) — men with a temple of Diana in their city. The denial Scripture treats is practical rather than philosophical: “The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. They are corrupt, they have done abominable works” (Psa 14:1; Psa 53:1). Paul's account is of suppression, not ignorance: “when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful” (Rom 1:21). And Jeremiah gives the exchange: “they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water” (Jer 2:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines atheist as one who disbelieves the existence of a God, or Supreme intelligent Being; and atheism as the disbelief of the existence of a God.
webster_full: ATHEIST, n. One who disbelieves the existence of a God, or Supreme intelligent Being.
2. A godless person.
ATHEISM, n. The disbelief of the existence of a God, or Supreme intelligent Being.
ATHEISTICAL, a. Pertaining to atheism; disbelieving the existence of a God; impious; applied to persons.
scriptures: Eph 2:12
That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world:
Psa 14:1
To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. They are corrupt, they have done abominable works, there is none that doeth good.
Rom 1:21
Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened.
Jer 2:13
For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
Psa 53:1
To the chief Musician upon Mahalath, Maschil, A Psalm of David. The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. Corrupt are they, and have done abominable iniquity: there is none that doeth good.
corruption_summary: Atheism is treated as a modern intellectual position, and Scripture's word for it lands on religious people.
corruption_paragraphs: Ephesians 2:12 is the surprise. Paul calls the Ephesians atheoi — godless — and Ephesus was one of the most religious cities in the empire, home to a temple counted among the wonders of the world. They had gods in abundance. What they did not have was God, and the biblical category is therefore not about the number of deities a man affirms but about whether he stands in any relation to the living One. On that definition a great deal of religion is atheism with furniture.

Psalm 14:1 is misquoted constantly by leaving out the location. The fool hath said in his heart — not in a lecture, not in an argument. And what follows is not a refutation but a description of conduct: they are corrupt, they have done abominable works, there is none that doeth good. The psalm treats practical atheism as the real problem, which is the thing every believer does whenever he acts as if God were not in the room. On that reading the verse's first application is inside the church, and it was David who wrote it about Israel.

This is not a licence to be dismissive of honest unbelief, and Christians who use the fool of Psalm 14 as a term of abuse have misread the psalm and disobeyed the Lord's warning about that word. Romans 1 says the problem is suppression rather than stupidity, and Jeremiah 2:13 says the man who leaves the fountain does not stop digging — he hews out cisterns, works hard at them, and they hold no water. That is a description of something exhausting and sad rather than contemptible, and it deserves the tone Paul used at Athens: argument, patience, and a real hearing given to the objection.
roots_summary: Greek atheos (G112), without God; Hebrew nabal (H5036), fool; ein Elohim (H430), there is no God; bor nishbar (H953), a broken cistern.
roots_lines: Greek atheos (G112) — without God, godless; Ephesians 2:12 only.
Hebrew nabal (H5036) — fool, one morally senseless; Psalm 14:1, 53:1, Isaiah 32:6, 1 Samuel 25:25.
Hebrew me'ayan mayim chayyim (H4726) — fountain of living waters; Jeremiah 2:13, 17:13, John 4:10–14.
usage: “Without God in the world” — said of men with a temple of Diana.
“The fool hath said in his heart” — in his heart, and then his conduct.
“Hewed them out cisterns” — exhausting work, holding no water.

pos: n. pl. (those who divide a church; makers of a breach where doctrine did not require one)
etymology: Greek schisma, a tear or rent, from schizo, to split — the word used of a rent garment and of the veil of the temple. Paul uses it of the Corinthian factions.
biblical_def: Schismatics tear the body. Paul's plea is against the thing by name: “that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you” (1Co 1:10) — schismata. The purpose of the body's design is stated: God tempered the body together, “that there should be no schism in the body; but that the members should have the same care one for another” (1Co 12:25). Those who cause it are to be marked: “mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them” (Rom 16:17). The factious man is refused after two warnings: “A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject” (Tit 3:10). And the duty is labour: “endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines schismatic as one who separates from an established church, on account of a diversity of opinions; and schism as a division or separation in a church, or a breach of unity among people of the same religious faith.
webster_full: SCHISM, n. In a general sense, division or separation; but appropriately, a division or separation in a church or denomination of christians, occasioned by diversity of opinions; breach of unity among people of the same religious faith.
SCHISMATIC, n. One who separates from an established church or religious faith, on account of a diversity of opinions.
scriptures: Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
That there should be no schism in the body; but that the members should have the same care one for another.
Now I beseech you, brethren, mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them.
Tit 3:10
A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject;
Eph 4:3
Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
corruption_summary: The charge is levelled at whoever leaves, and Scripture more often lays it on those who made leaving necessary.
corruption_paragraphs: Schism is a real sin and the New Testament treats it seriously; a congregation split over personality, style, or a leader's wounded pride has done something Paul spends a whole letter opposing. But the label is nearly always applied by the party in possession, and Romans 16:17 does not read that way. Mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned — the standard is the doctrine, not the address. On that measure the schismatic may be the man who stayed and changed what was taught, and the ones who left may be the ones who kept it.

This is precisely the Reformers' defence, and it must be stated or the whole tradition is indefensible. Charged with rending the church, they answered that they had not left the church but the corruptions, that the marks of a true church are the word rightly preached and the sacraments rightly administered, and that where those are gone the separation has already happened. The 1689 stands in that line. A tradition born of separation has no business treating separation as unthinkable — and equally no business treating it as cheap, which is the modern failure.

First Corinthians 12:25 gives the positive reason unity matters and it is not organisational. God tempered the body together that there should be no schism in the body; but that the members should have the same care one for another — the alternative to schism is mutual care rather than mere co-existence. That is why Ephesians 4:3 uses a word of exertion: endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit. The unity already exists, being the Spirit's; what is commanded is the labour of not tearing it, and the labour is real, unglamorous, and mostly consists of bearing with people.
roots_summary: Greek schisma (G4978), a rent, division; hairetikos (G141), factious, heretical; dichostasia (G1370), division, sedition; henotes (G1775), unity.
roots_lines: Greek schisma (G4978) — a rent, division; 1 Corinthians 1:10, 11:18, 12:25, and of a garment, Matthew 9:16.
Greek hairetikos (G141) — factious, party-making; Titus 3:10 only.
Greek dichostasia (G1370) — division; Romans 16:17, Galatians 5:20, 1 Corinthians 3:3.
usage: “That there be no divisions among you” — and the word is schismata.
“Contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned” — the standard is doctrine, not address.
“Endeavouring to keep the unity” — a word of exertion.

pos: n. (the office of deacon; the second of the two New Testament church offices)
etymology: Greek diakonos, a servant, one who waits at table. The word is used of Christ Himself, of civil rulers, and of Paul's own ministry before it names an office.
biblical_def: The diaconate is the office of service in the church. It is instituted to meet a real need: “look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business” (Act 6:3). It is named alongside the eldership and nowhere else: “to all the saints in Christ Jesus which are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons” (Php 1:1). Its qualifications are moral: “Likewise must the deacons be grave, not doubletongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre” (1Ti 3:8). Phebe is commended as “a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea” (Rom 16:1). And faithful service is itself the promotion: “they that have used the office of a deacon well purchase to themselves a good degree” (1Ti 3:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines deacon as a person in the lowest degree of holy orders; and, in the Presbyterian and Independent churches, an officer whose business is to attend to the secular affairs of the church and the relief of the poor.
webster_full: DEACON, n. A person in the lowest degree of holy orders.
The deacon's office was to serve tables, the sacred feast, and the agape, and to distribute bread and wine to the communicants.
2. In the Presbyterian and Independent churches, a person whose business is to attend to the secular affairs of the church, to relieve the poor, and to distribute the elements.
DEACONSHIP, n. The office or ministry of a deacon.
scriptures: Act 6:3
Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.
Php 1:1
Paul and Timotheus, the servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus which are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons:
Likewise must the deacons be grave, not doubletongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre;
Rom 16:1
I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea:
For they that have used the office of a deacon well purchase to themselves a good degree, and great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: The diaconate is treated as a training grade for the eldership, and Scripture gives it as an office complete in itself.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest Protestant error is to regard deacons as junior elders, which turns a distinct office into a waiting room and dissolves the point of having two. The New Testament separates the work cleanly: the apostles refused to leave the word of God and serve tables, and created an office so that neither would be neglected. Both were necessary; that is the whole reason for the arrangement. First Timothy 3:13 says a man who serves well in this office purchases to himself a good degree and great boldness — the advancement is in standing and confidence, not in a promotion elsewhere.

Acts 6 also shows what the office is for, and it is worth stating plainly because the qualifications sound almost excessive for the task. The complaint was that the Grecian widows were neglected in the daily ministration — a matter of food, favouritism and ethnic tension inside a congregation. The apostles asked for men full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom to handle it. Money, mercy and fairness among people who feel overlooked require more spiritual maturity than the church usually assumes, not less, and every one of the seven named has a Greek name, which suggests the aggrieved party was given the administration.

Romans 16:1 has been argued over for centuries and the honest thing is to say what is and is not clear. The word used of Phebe is diakonos, the same word rendered deacon elsewhere, and Paul commends her as a succourer of many and of himself; 1 Timothy 3:11 refers to women in the middle of the deacon qualifications. This dictionary holds a complementarian reading of the teaching and ruling office and notes that the diaconate is not that office. Whatever a church concludes about the title, it should be able to say how the mercy ministry of its women is recognised, because Paul thought Phebe worth naming first in a chapter of greetings.
roots_summary: Greek diakonos (G1249), servant, deacon; diakoneo (G1247), to serve; diakonia (G1248), ministry, service; bathmos (G898), a step, degree.
roots_lines: Greek diakonos (G1249) — deacon, servant; Philippians 1:1, 1 Timothy 3:8–12, Romans 16:1; of Christ, Romans 15:8.
Greek diakonia (G1248) — ministration, service; Acts 6:1, 6:4, 2 Corinthians 8:4, 9:1.
Greek bathmos kalos (G898) — a good degree, a good standing; 1 Timothy 3:13 only.
usage: “Full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom” — asked for, to distribute food.
“With the bishops and deacons” — two offices, and no third.
“Purchase to themselves a good degree” — in standing, not elsewhere.

pos: n. pl. (the heads of monasteries; superiors of religious houses, styled “father”)
etymology: Aramaic abba, father, through Greek and Latin abbas — the very word Christ used in Gethsemane and the word the Spirit puts in the believer's mouth. The title of the office is the Bible's most intimate name for God.
biblical_def: An abbot is the head of a monastery, and his title is the Aramaic word for father. In Scripture that word belongs to two speakers. Christ, in the garden: “Abba, Father, all things are possible unto thee; take away this cup from me: nevertheless not what I will, but what thou wilt” (Mar 14:36). And the adopted believer: “ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father” (Rom 8:15); “God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father” (Gal 4:6). Against its use as a rank the Lord is explicit: “call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven” (Mat 23:9), in the same passage as “all ye are brethren” (Mat 23:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines abbot as the superior or governor of an abbey or monastery; and notes the word is from the Syriac or Chaldee abba, father.
webster_full: ABBOT, n. The superior or governor of an abbey or monastery.
Originally the name was given to any aged monk; but it was afterwards appropriated to the head of the house.
ABBA, n. In the Chaldee and Syriac, a father, and figuratively a superior.
ABBEY, n. A monastery or society of persons of either sex, secluded from the world and devoted to religion.
scriptures: And he said, Abba, Father, all things are possible unto thee; take away this cup from me: nevertheless not what I will, but what thou wilt.
Rom 8:15
For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father.
Gal 4:6
And because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father.
Mat 23:9
And call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven.
Mat 23:8
But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren.
corruption_summary: The most intimate name a Christian has for God was made into an ecclesiastical rank.
corruption_paragraphs: The etymology carries the whole objection and no polemic is needed to make it. Abba occurs three times in the New Testament: once from the lips of the Son in Gethsemane, and twice of what the Spirit produces in a believer's heart. It is not a formal word; it is the word a child uses. That this became the title of an office, conferred by appointment and attaching to a man's rank rather than to a relationship, is a loss whatever one concludes about monasteries. Matthew 23:9 forbids exactly this transfer — call no man your father upon the earth — and gives the reason: one is your Father, which is in heaven.

The prohibition is not wooden and reading it so produces absurdities, since Paul calls himself a father to the Corinthians and to Timothy, and Scripture is full of honoured fathers. What the Lord forbids in that passage is a class of religious titles — Rabbi, father, master — that place men above the brotherhood and locate in them what belongs to God. The governing clause is all ye are brethren, and the test for any title is whether it operates inside that or above it.

Romans 8:15 shows what the church gave away. The Spirit of adoption is contrasted with the spirit of bondage again to fear, and the mark of the difference is the cry: Abba, Father. A believer who has been taught to approach God through a hierarchy of fathers has been given back the bondage the verse says he was delivered from, however kindly the intermediaries behave. And the same word is on the Son's lips at the worst hour of His life, which is the strongest evidence in Scripture that a man in extremity may speak to God directly, and as a child.
roots_summary: Aramaic abba (G5), father; Greek pater (G3962), father; huiothesia (G5206), adoption; adelphoi (G80), brethren.
roots_lines: Aramaic abba (G5) — father; Mark 14:36, Romans 8:15, Galatians 4:6 — all three occurrences, each paired with pater.
Greek huiothesia (G5206) — adoption as sons; Romans 8:15, 8:23, Galatians 4:5, Ephesians 1:5.
Greek pater (G3962) — father; Matthew 23:9, and of God, Matthew 6:9.
usage: “Abba, Father… nevertheless not what I will” — in the garden.
“Whereby we cry, Abba, Father” — what the Spirit produces.
“One is your Father, which is in heaven” — and all ye are brethren.

pos: n. (the theological faculty of the University of Paris; in Calvin, the type of a learned body that has lost the gospel)
etymology: Founded by Robert de Sorbon in 1257. By Calvin's day — he had studied in Paris — it was the arbiter of orthodoxy in France, and it condemned Luther's writings in 1521.
biblical_def: The Sorbonne stands in Calvin's writing for theological learning that has become an authority over the text rather than a servant of it. Scripture's warnings are exact: “Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?” (1Co 1:20); “beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit” (Col 2:8); “avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called” (1Ti 6:20). The saddest description is of men who never arrive: “Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth” (2Ti 3:7). And the Pharisees' argument from the faculty is recorded without an answer: “Have any of the rulers or of the Pharisees believed on him?” (John 7:48).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Sorbonne; his definition of divinity as a discipline is the relevant one: the science of divine things; the science which unfolds the character of God, his laws and moral government.
webster_full: DIVINITY, n. The science of divine things; the science which unfolds the character of God, his laws and moral government, the duties of man, and the way of salvation; theology.
SCHOOL, n. A place or house in which persons are instructed in arts, science, languages or any species of learning.
2. The learners in a school or seminary of learning, considered as an assemblage.
scriptures: Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called:
Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.
John 7:48
Have any of the rulers or of the Pharisees believed on him?
corruption_summary: Institutional learning is trusted as a guarantee of orthodoxy, and every faculty that ever went wrong had the credentials.
corruption_paragraphs: John 7:48 is the argument from the faculty in its purest form, and the Gospel records it without a rebuttal: Have any of the rulers or of the Pharisees believed on him? The answer at that moment was almost none — Nicodemus is in the room and says something cautious. The argument is not stupid; deferring to the people who have studied a subject is ordinarily sound. What the verse establishes is that it can fail completely, and that a whole learned class can be wrong about the most important question ever put to it while remaining learned.

Nothing here is an argument against theological education, which the Reformed have always built at the first opportunity — Geneva's Academy was Calvin's own work, and the tradition has produced institutions rather than despised them. The point is that a faculty is a means and not a guarantee. The Sorbonne of the sixteenth century was the most rigorous theological body in Europe and it condemned the recovery of the doctrine of justification. Rigour is not the same as fidelity, and a man may be trained to argue exactly for a conclusion that is exactly wrong.

Second Timothy 3:7 names the peculiar failure of institutions rather than individuals: ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth. The learning is real and continuous, and it arrives nowhere, because knowledge in the biblical sense is not the accumulation of data about God but an acquaintance with Him. The safeguard is the one 1 Timothy 6:20 gives — keep that which is committed to thy trust — a deposit received and handed on intact, which is a humbler description of the theologian's job than any faculty has ever liked.
roots_summary: Greek grammateus (G1122), scribe; suzetetes (G4804), disputer; pseudonumos gnosis (G5581, G1108), science falsely so called; paratheke (G3866), a deposit committed in trust.
roots_lines: Greek suzetetes tou aionos toutou (G4804) — the disputer of this world; 1 Corinthians 1:20.
Greek pseudonumos gnosis (G5581) — knowledge falsely so called; 1 Timothy 6:20 only.
Greek paratheke (G3866) — the deposit committed; 1 Timothy 6:20, 2 Timothy 1:12, 1:14.
usage: “Have any of the rulers… believed on him?” — recorded without a rebuttal.
“Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth”.
“Keep that which is committed to thy trust” — a deposit, handed on intact.

pos: v. (to renounce upon oath; to deny or disavow with a solemn asseveration)
etymology: Latin abjurare, to deny on oath, from ab-, away, and jurare, to swear. The word belongs to the persecutions: an accused Christian was required to abjure, and the formula was usually short.
biblical_def: To abjure is to renounce under oath. Peter did it: “And again he denied with an oath, I do not know the man” (Mat 26:72). The Lord states what hangs on it: “whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father which is in heaven” (Mat 10:33); and Paul repeats it: “if we deny him, he also will deny us” (2Ti 2:12). The apostles' refusal before the council is the counter-formula: “Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye. For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” (Act 4:19–20). And the church at Pergamos is commended for holding fast: “hast not denied my faith, even in those days wherein Antipas was my faithful martyr” (Rev 2:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines abjure as to renounce upon oath; to abandon; and, in a general sense, to reject with solemnity; to renounce or reject with abhorrence.
webster_full: ABJURE, v.t. To renounce upon oath; to abandon.
2. To renounce, discard or deny.
ABJURATION, n. The act of abjuring; a renunciation upon oath; as, an abjuration of the realm, by which a person swears to leave the country forever.
2. A rejection or denial with solemnity; a total abandonment.
scriptures: And again he denied with an oath, I do not know the man.
But whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father which is in heaven.
If we suffer, we shall also reign with him: if we deny him, he also will deny us:
Act 4:19
But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.
Rev 2:13

I know thy works, and where thou dwellest, even where Satan's seat is: and thou holdest fast my name, and hast not denied my faith, even in those days wherein Antipas was my faithful martyr, who was slain among you, where Satan dwelleth.
corruption_summary: Denial is imagined as a decision made under torture, and Peter's was made by a fire, to a servant girl.
corruption_paragraphs: The circumstances of the most famous denial in history are worth holding in view whenever a Christian wonders how he would do under persecution. Peter was not before a tribunal. He was warming himself at a fire in a courtyard, and the person who identified him was a maid. There was no torture, no formal charge, and no immediate threat of death — and this was a man who a few hours earlier had drawn a sword against an armed party and meant it. Courage in a crisis and courage in a conversation are not the same faculty, and the second fails more often.

The passage that terrifies is Matthew 10:33, and it must be read with the case beside it. Peter denied Christ three times, with an oath and with cursing, and was restored by name at a fire on a beach with a threefold question — and preached at Pentecost. So the warning cannot mean that a single failure is final; the Gospel that records the warning also records the restoration. What Matthew 10 describes is a settled disowning rather than a collapse repented of, and the difference between Peter and Judas is not the size of the sin but where each took it afterwards.

Revelation 2:13 gives the commendation in the language of ordinary faithfulness under real pressure: thou holdest fast my name, and hast not denied my faith, even in those days wherein Antipas was my faithful martyr, who was slain among you. The church at Pergamos had watched a man die and had gone on confessing. Nothing in the verse suggests they found it easy or that they were remarkable in any other respect — the same letter has hard things to say to them. They simply did not abjure, and the Lord names it first.
roots_summary: Greek arneomai (G720), to deny, disown; aparneomai (G533), to deny utterly; homologeo (G3670), to confess; krateo (G2902), to hold fast.
roots_lines: Greek arneomai (G720) — to deny, disown; Matthew 26:70–72, 10:33, 2 Timothy 2:12, Titus 1:16.
Greek homologeo (G3670) — to confess, say the same thing; Matthew 10:32, Romans 10:9, 1 John 1:9.
Greek krateo (G2902) — to hold fast; Revelation 2:13, 2:25, 3:11, Hebrews 4:14.
usage: “He denied with an oath” — by a fire, to a servant girl.
“We cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” — the counter-formula.
“Hast not denied my faith” — and they had watched Antipas die.

pos: adj. (fair in appearance but not in reality; plausible without being true)
etymology: Latin speciosus, good-looking, from species, appearance. The word once meant simply beautiful; it soured because so much that looks right is not.
biblical_def: A specious thing looks right and is not. Paul warns of the technique: “this I say, lest any man should beguile you with enticing words” (Col 2:4), and names its operators: “by good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple” (Rom 16:18). The disguise runs to the top: “Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light” (2Co 11:14). The Lord's version is a costume: false prophets “come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves” (Mat 7:15). And Proverbs applies it to a man's own reasoning, which is where it does most damage: “There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death” (Pro 14:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines specious as apparently right; superficially fair, just or correct; plausible; appearing well at first view.
webster_full: SPECIOUS, a. Showy; pleasing to the view.
The rest, far greater part, will deem in outward rites and specious forms religion satisfied.
2. Apparently right; superficially fair, just or correct; plausible; appearing well at first view; as specious reasoning; a specious argument.
SPECIOUSLY, adv. With a fair appearance; with show of right.
scriptures: Col 2:4
And this I say, lest any man should beguile you with enticing words.
For they that are such serve not our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly; and by good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple.
And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light.
Mat 7:15
Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.
There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.
corruption_summary: The specious argument is expected to come from an opponent, and Proverbs locates it inside the man's own head.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 14:12 is the verse that makes this doctrine personal, and it appears twice in the book because it is worth saying twice. There is a way which seemeth right unto a man — not which a deceiver sells him, but which looks right from where he stands — and the end thereof are the ways of death. The most dangerous specious reasoning a Christian meets is his own, produced by a mind with an interest in the conclusion, and it arrives with all the marks of good sense because it was manufactured by the faculty that recognises good sense.

Romans 16:18 names the mechanism and the target with unusual bluntness: by good words and fair speeches they deceive the hearts of the simple. Not the wicked, and not the stupid — the guileless, the ones who assume that people mean what they say. That is why Paul's remedy in the next verse is not suspicion but a division of labour in the mind: I would have you wise unto that which is good, and simple concerning evil. Innocence about how to do harm, and shrewdness about how it is done to you.

Webster's first illustration is worth the entry on its own, and it names the religious form: the rest, far greater part, will deem in outward rites and specious forms religion satisfied. A specious religion is the hardest kind to leave, because it supplies everything except the thing itself — the meetings, the vocabulary, the moral seriousness, the sense of belonging. Second Corinthians 11:14 explains why: the disguise is always toward the light. Nothing that presents itself as darkness would ever get a hearing in a church.
roots_summary: Greek pithanologia (G4086), persuasive speech, enticing words; chrestologia (G5542), fair speaking; metaschematizo (G3345), to transform in appearance; akakos (G172), simple, without guile.
roots_lines: Greek pithanologia (G4086) — persuasive but false speech; Colossians 2:4 only.
Greek chrestologia (G5542) — smooth, plausible talk; Romans 16:18 only.
Greek akakos (G172) — guileless, simple; Romans 16:18, Hebrews 7:26 — where it is said of Christ.
usage: “A way which seemeth right unto a man” — and he built it himself.
“Deceive the hearts of the simple” — the guileless, not the stupid.
“Wise unto that which is good, and simple concerning evil” — the division of labour.

pos: adj. (wicked in the extreme; atrociously villainous)
etymology: Latin nefarius, from ne-, not, and fas, divine law — that which is against what is permitted by heaven. The word names not merely a crime but an offence against the order of things.
biblical_def: A nefarious act is wickedness of the deliberate, inventive kind. Genesis gives the pre-flood verdict: “God saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually” (Gen 6:5). Paul lists the faculty among the fruits of a reprobate mind: “inventors of evil things” (Rom 1:30). Proverbs puts the designing heart among the seven abominations: “an heart that deviseth wicked imaginations, feet that be swift in running to mischief” (Pro 6:18). Micah shows the planning: “Woe to them that devise iniquity, and work evil upon their beds! when the morning is light, they practise it” (Mic 2:1). And the trajectory is downward: “evil men and seducers shall wax worse and worse, deceiving, and being deceived” (2Ti 3:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines nefarious as wicked in the extreme; abominable; atrociously villainous; detestably vile.
webster_full: NEFARIOUS, a. Wicked in the extreme; abominable; atrociously villainous; execrable; detestably vile.
NEFARIOUSLY, adv. With extreme wickedness; abominably.
scriptures: Gen 6:5
And GOD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.
Rom 1:30
Backbiters, haters of God, despiteful, proud, boasters, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents,
Pro 6:18
An heart that deviseth wicked imaginations, feet that be swift in running to mischief,
Mic 2:1
Woe to them that devise iniquity, and work evil upon their beds! when the morning is light, they practise it, because it is in the power of their hand.
But evil men and seducers shall wax worse and worse, deceiving, and being deceived.
corruption_summary: Extreme wickedness is treated as a different species from ordinary sin, and Scripture describes the same root inventing new fruit.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 1:30 contains a phrase that sits oddly in its list and is easy to read past: inventors of evil things. Between the disobedient to parents and the covenantbreakers stands a description of creativity. Depravity in Scripture is not merely a failure to reach a standard; it is productive, generating forms of evil that had to be thought of. Genesis 6:5 says the same thing about the antediluvian world with the word imagination — every imagination of the thoughts of his heart only evil continually. The faculty that makes men able to build cathedrals is the faculty that designs the machinery of a persecution.

Micah 2:1 supplies the detail that separates the nefarious from the impulsive, and it is domestic: they work evil upon their beds, and when the morning is light, they practise it. The planning happens in private, at night, by men who then get up and go about it in the ordinary hours. The prophet is describing property fraud in the following verse — they covet fields, and take them by violence — which is a useful corrective to the idea that extreme wickedness is exotic. Most of it is done in daylight by men with a plan.

The Reformed doctrine of depravity is the only account that makes sense of the twentieth century without either despairing of human nature or excusing it. Men who were educated, cultured and personally polite designed and administered atrocities, and no theory of ignorance or deprivation explains it. Second Timothy 3:13 says the movement is downward — worse and worse, deceiving and being deceived — because a man who authors evil is also consumed by it. That is the sober half. The other half is that the same doctrine, applied honestly, forbids anyone to locate the capacity only in other people.
roots_summary: Hebrew yetser (H3336), imagination, formed purpose; chashab (H2803), to devise; Greek epheuretes kakon (G2182), inventors of evil things; goes (G1114), a seducer, impostor.
roots_lines: Hebrew yetser machshevoth libbo (H3336) — the imagination of the thoughts of his heart; Genesis 6:5, 8:21, 1 Chronicles 28:9.
Greek epheuretai kakon (G2182) — inventors of evil things; Romans 1:30 only.
Hebrew choshvey aven (H2803) — devisers of iniquity; Micah 2:1, Proverbs 6:18, Psalm 36:4.
usage: “Inventors of evil things” — a description of creativity, in that list.
“Work evil upon their beds… when the morning is light, they practise it”.
“Deceiving, and being deceived” — the author is consumed too.

pos: n. (fitness; accuracy; conformity to what is proper to a thing, an office or an occasion)
etymology: Latin proprietas, ownness, from proprius, one's own. Propriety is not politeness; it is the quality of a thing being proper to its subject — the right word, the right conduct, for this and not another.
biblical_def: Propriety is fitness to the case. Proverbs prizes it in speech: “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver” (Pro 25:11), and again, “a word spoken in due season, how good is it!” (Pro 15:23). Paul makes it a rule of conduct: “that women adorn themselves in modest apparel… which becometh women professing godliness” (1Ti 2:9–10), and of doctrine: “speak thou the things which become sound doctrine” (Tit 2:1). Of the assembly he says only, “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40). And Proverbs notes what is not fitting: “Delight is not seemly for a fool; much less for a servant to have rule over princes” (Pro 19:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines propriety as fitness; suitableness; appropriateness; consonance with established principles, rules or customs; and accuracy, justness, as of words or language.
webster_full: PROPRIETY, n. Property; peculiar or exclusive right of possession. [Obs.]
2. Fitness; suitableness; appropriateness; consonance with established principles, rules or customs; justness; accuracy.
Propriety of thought is that which is truly conformable to the subject.
Propriety of words is the peculiar and exclusive use of them to express a certain idea.
scriptures: A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.
A man hath joy by the answer of his mouth: and a word spoken in due season, how good is it!
In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;
Tit 2:1
But speak thou the things which become sound doctrine:
Let all things be done decently and in order.
corruption_summary: Propriety is reduced to social convention, and Webster's own definition makes it a matter of truth: what is conformable to the subject.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster's line is the best short account of the word in English and it is not about manners at all: propriety of thought is that which is truly conformable to the subject. A proper word is one that fits the thing it names; a proper action is one that fits the case it answers. That makes propriety a species of honesty rather than of etiquette, and explains why Scripture treats it seriously. To speak of a grief in the language of a trifle, or of a trifle in the language of a grief, is a small lie about the world.

Proverbs 25:11 gives the picture and the emphasis falls on the adverb: a word fitly spoken. Not a true word merely, and not a kind word merely — the right word, at the right moment, in the right weight. Proverbs 15:23 adds the timing: a word spoken in due season, how good is it. Anyone who has been comforted well, or corrected well, knows that the content was often unremarkable and the fitness was everything; and anyone who has said the true thing at the wrong hour knows the cost.

The corruption to guard against is the use of propriety as a shield. Congregations have used it to silence honest grief, to forbid uncomfortable questions, and to enforce cultural preferences that have nothing to do with the gospel — and a great deal of what passes for decorum in church is simply the taste of whoever has been there longest. The test is Titus 2:1: speak the things which become sound doctrine. The standard is the doctrine, and a propriety that cannot be traced back to it is a custom, which may be kept or dropped as charity requires.
roots_summary: Hebrew ophan (H655), fitly, in due manner; eth (H6256), season, time; Greek prepo (G4241), to be becoming; euschemonos (G2156), decently, becomingly.
roots_lines: Hebrew al-ophnav (H655) — fitly, upon its wheels, in due manner; Proverbs 25:11 only.
Greek prepo (G4241) — to be fitting, becoming; 1 Timothy 2:10, Titus 2:1, Ephesians 5:3, Hebrews 7:26.
Greek euschemonos (G2156) — decently, becomingly; 1 Corinthians 14:40, Romans 13:13, 1 Thessalonians 4:12.
usage: “A word fitly spoken” — and the adverb carries it.
“Which become sound doctrine” — the standard, not the custom.
“A word spoken in due season, how good is it!”
